entities.summary:
Vox, founded in 2013 by Santiago Abascal and former People's Party politicians dissatisfied with the PP's centrist drift, became the third-largest party in the Spanish Congress of Deputies in 2019 elections — ending Spain's 40-year post-Franco democratic consensus that had excluded far-right parties from government. Vox's entry into the Andalusian regional coalition (2019) was the first time a far-right party entered Spanish government since Franco's death, marking the end of the exceptional Spanish democratic taboo on far-right governance.

Vox was founded by Santiago Abascal and other PP politicians who believed the party was too willing to compromise with Catalan and Basque nationalism and insufficiently conservative on social issues. The party's breakthrough came in the December 2018 Andalusian elections (the party's first regional representation) and 2019 general elections (52 seats). Vox campaigns against Catalan independence, immigration, Islam, abortion rights, gender equality laws, and the 2007 Historical Memory Law — which recognized Franco-era victims.

Vox's most distinctive policy is its opposition to Spain's autonomous community system — arguing for recentralization that would abolish regional self-government as a response to Catalan independence demands. The party's entry into the Castilla y León regional government coalition with the PP (2022) and national coalition talks in 2023 (when PP won elections but lacked majority) demonstrated how far-right parties in Southern Europe can shift governing coalitions. Vox has become the reference point for Spanish-speaking populist right parties in Latin America.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Vox's 2019 breakthrough ended Spain's unique post-Franco democratic taboo on far-right participation in government — the 40-year consensus that had distinguished Spanish democracy from France, Italy, and Austria — marking the normalization of far-right politics across the entire European South.
